Our final exam is on Friday May 1 from 2pm to 5pm in Griffith Theater (our usual classroom). Here's what you need to know:

- The exam is all multiple choice;
- The exam is similar in style and format to the in-class components of the two midterms;
- The exam should not take the full three hours to complete;
- The only resource you are allowed is both sides of a single 8.5" x 11" sheet of notes (prepared however you want);
- The exam is cumulative, with slightly disproportionate emphasis on our last topic, statistical inference;
- I can just tell you right now that webscraping will not appear on the exam, so don't even worry about it.

The study advice [here](https://edstem.org/us/courses/90224/discussion/7626328) still applies. Below are 47 new practice problems to sink your teeth into, but because the final exam is cumulative, the study guides for Midterms [1](/exams/midterm-1.html) and [2](/exams/midterm-2.html) remain very relevant. You should regard the *true* final exam study guide as the "full join" of all three guides.

::: callout-tip
## Try this first

To start, attempt all of the problems below *without resources*. Make note of your pain points and blind spots along the way. That might give you an idea of the stuff you would benefit from if you had it on a cheat sheet.
:::

### Question `{r} q_no`


Match the histogram to the set of numerical summaries. There is exactly one unique match for each.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-asp: 0.8

set.seed(12345)

n_fig <- 6
n <- 3000

d <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.75)

x1 <- rnorm(n)
x2 <- rexp(n) - 4
x3 <- -rexp(n) + 4
x4 <- d * rnorm(n, -3, 0.5) + (1 - d) * rnorm(n, 2, 0.5)
x5 <- runif(n, 0, 4)
x6 <- rnorm(n, -3, 0.4)

hist_match <- tibble(
  hist = sort(rep(c("i", "ii", "iii", "iv", "v", "vi"), n)),
  x = c(x1, x2, x6, x4, x5, x3)
)

# plot histograms

ggplot(hist_match, aes(x = x)) + 
  geom_histogram() +
  facet_wrap(~hist)

# plot answer choices

hist_match |>
  group_by(hist) |>
  summarize(
    mean = mean(x),
    median = median(x),
    `standard deviation` = sd(x)
  ) |>
  slice(sample(1:n())) |>
  add_column(
    choice = c("a", "b", "c", "d", "e", "f")
  ) |>
  relocate(choice) |>
  select(!hist) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 1)
```

### Question `{r} q_no`


```{r}
#| echo: false
set.seed(1234567)
my_colors <- c("red", "blue", "forestgreen")
subsamps <- c(10, 20, 35)
b0 <- 12 + c(2, 6, -3)
b1 <- c(1, 5, -0.2)

y <- c()
x <- c()
cl <- c()

for(i in 1:length(my_colors)){
  x_sub <- rnorm(subsamps[i], 4, 1)
  y <- c(y, b0[i] + b1[i] * x_sub + rnorm(subsamps[i], 0, 1))
  x <- c(x, x_sub)
  cl <- c(cl, rep(my_colors[i], subsamps[i]))
}

df <- tibble(
  x = x, y = y, color = fct_relevel(cl, my_colors)
)
df <- df[sample(1:nrow(df)), ]
```

Here's a nonsense dataset that I made up:

```{r}
glimpse(df)
```

Imagine you run this code:

```{r}
#| eval: false
linear_reg() |>
  fit(y ~ x + color, df) |>
  tidy()
```

The output would be a lil' table like this:

::: {.center-table}
| `term` | `estimate` | 
|---------|:-----|
| `(Intercept)`      | $b_0$   |   
| `x`     | $b_1$  |  
| `colorblue`       | $b_2$   |   
| `colorforestgreen`       | $b_3$    |   
:::

A plot of the model fit might look something like this:

```{r}
#| fig-asp: 1
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center

add_slope_wedge <- function(intercept, slope, x0,
                            run = NULL,       # horizontal length of wedge
                            cex = 1,          # text size
                            col = "black",
                            lwd = 2,
                            label = TRUE) {

  # If run not supplied, choose something that looks reasonable
  if (is.null(run)) {
    usr <- par("usr")              # current plot limits
    run <- 0.08 * (usr[2] - usr[1])
  }
  
  # Point on the line where wedge attaches
  y0 <- intercept + slope * x0
  
  # End of horizontal "run"
  x1 <- x0 + run
  y1 <- y0
  
  # Vertical "rise"
  rise <- slope * run
  x2 <- x1
  y2 <- y1 + rise
  
  # Draw the triangle edges
  segments(x0, y0, x1, y1, col = col, lwd = lwd)  # run
  segments(x1, y1, x2, y2, col = col, lwd = lwd)  # rise
  segments(x0, y0, x2, y2, col = col, lwd = lwd)  # hypotenuse (optional but nice)
  
  # Optional labels
  if (label) {
    text((x0 + x1)/2, y0, "run", pos = 1, cex = cex, col = col)
    text(x1, (y1 + y2)/2, "rise", pos = 4, cex = cex, col = col)
  }
}

my_fit <- linear_reg() |>
  fit(y ~ x + color, df) |>
  tidy()

cepts <- c(my_fit$estimate[1], my_fit$estimate[1] + my_fit$estimate[3], my_fit$estimate[1] + my_fit$estimate[4])
slope <- my_fit$estimate[2]

plot(x, y, col = cl, pch = 19, xaxt = "n", yaxt = "n", bty = "n", xlim = c(-4, 1.4 * max(x)), ylim = c(-5, max(y)), cex = 1)
add_slope_wedge(cepts[1], slope, 7, label = FALSE)
add_slope_wedge(cepts[2], slope, 7, label = FALSE)
add_slope_wedge(cepts[3], slope, 7, label = FALSE)
abline(v = 0, lwd = 2)
abline(h = 0, lwd = 2)
abline(a = cepts[1], b = slope, col = my_colors[1], lwd = 2)
abline(a = cepts[2], b = slope, col = my_colors[2], lwd = 2)
abline(a = cepts[3], b = slope, col = my_colors[3], lwd = 2)
points(numeric(length(cepts)), 
       cepts, 
       cex = 2, pch = 19)
arrows(-1, 0.95 * cepts[2] + slope * (-1), -1, 1.1 * cepts[1] + slope * (-1), lwd = 2, code = 3)
arrows(-1, 0.95 * cepts[1] + slope * (-1), -1, 1.1 * cepts[3] + slope * (-1), lwd = 2, code = 3)
arrows(-3, 0.95 * cepts[2] + slope * (-3), -3, 1.1 * cepts[3] + slope * (-3), lwd = 2, code = 3)


#text(0.5, 1.5 + cepts[2] + slope * 0.5, "IV")

text(-4, 0.5*cepts[1] + 0.5*cepts[2], "I")
text(-2, 0.5*cepts[1] + 0.5*cepts[2], "II")
text(-2, 0.5*cepts[1] + 0.5*cepts[3], "III")

text(0.5, 1.5 + cepts[2] + slope * 0.5, "IV")
text(0.5, 1.5 + cepts[1] + slope * 0.5, "V")
text(0.5, 1.5 + cepts[3] + slope * 0.5, "VI")

text(7.5, cepts[2] + slope * 7 - 2, "VII")
text(7.5, cepts[1] + slope * 7 - 2, "VIII")
text(7.5, cepts[3] + slope * 7 - 2, "IX")
```

# Stat doctor 

Recall the Pokémon data from [AE 23](/ae/ae-23-pokemon-infer.html):

```{r}
#| message: false
pokemon <- read_csv("data/pokemon.csv") |>
  mutate(
    is_legendary = as_factor(is_legendary)
  )

glimpse(pokemon)
```

In 1999 my mom took me to see [*Pokémon: The First Movie*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pokémon:_The_First_Movie) in the theater, but apart from that, I don't actually know that much about Pokémon. At some point in the recent past, my little brother informed me that the new generations of Pokémon include a fellow named Garbodor:

![](images/garbodor.jpg){fig-align="center"}

With all due respect to Garbodor, this news did somewhat blunt my interest in Pokémon going forward. 

Anyway, below are several failed attempts at interpreting statistical results for these data. Diagnose the problem and fix it if possible.

#| include: false
q_no <- q_no + 1
```

```

### Question `{r} q_no`

```{r}
set.seed(12345)

pokemon |>
  specify(speed ~ defense) |>
  generate(reps = 500, type = "bootstrap") |>
  fit() |>
  get_confidence_interval(
    point_estimate = observed_fit,
    level = 0.9,
    type = "percentile"
  ) |>
  filter(term == "defense")
```

> We are confident that 95% of our data lies between -0.065 and 0.046.

```{r}
#| include: false
q_no <- q_no + 1
```

### Question `{r} q_no`

```{r}
set.seed(24601)

pokemon |>
  specify(speed ~ defense) |>
  hypothesize(null = "independence") |>
  generate(reps = 500, type = "permute") |>
  fit() |>
  get_p_value(obs_stat = observed_fit, direction = "two-sided")

```

> The probability that the null hypothesis is true (meaning `defense` and `speed` are uncorrelated) is about 53%.

```{r}
#| include: false
q_no <- q_no + 1
```

### Question `{r} q_no`

> Because the p-value is greater than 50%, we reject the alternative hypothesis. 

# Data analysis

## Duke Forest homes

```{r}
#| include: false
duke_forest <- openintro::duke_forest |>
  mutate(
    cooling = if_else(cooling == "central", "Central", "Non-central"),
    cooling = fct_relevel(cooling, "Non-central", "Central")
  ) |>
  select(-address, -type, -hoa, -url)
```

In this part of the exam you'll work with a dataset you've seen before: sale prices and other features of `{r} nrow(duke_forest)` homes in Duke Forest.
The data come from Zillow.
The name of the data frame is `duke_forest` and it contains the variables described in the table below.

| Variable     | Description                                            |
|:-------------|:-------------------------------------------------------|
| `price`      | Sale price, in USD                                     |
| `bed`        | Number of bedrooms                                     |
| `bath`       | Number of bathrooms                                    |
| `area`       | Area of home, in square feet                           |
| `year_built` | Year the home was built                                |
| `heating`    | Heating sytem                                          |
| `cooling`    | Cooling system (`Central` or `Non-central`)            |
| `parking`    | Type of parking available and number of parking spaces |
| `lot`        | Area of the entire property, in acres                  |

: {tbl-colwidths="\[20,80\]"}

A peek at the data is shown below.

```{r}
#| echo: false
options(width=70)
duke_forest
```

Suppose you're working in a team of three students, exploring and modeling prices of homes in Duke Forest. During your initial exploration, your team finds out that only a small number of homes in your sample have very few or very many bedrooms -- only 4 homes with 2 bedrooms, 30 with 3 bedrooms, 52 with 4 bedrooms, 11 with 5 bedrooms, and just 1 with 6 bedrooms.

Therefore, you decide to create a new variable, called `bed_new`, with the following logic:

-   If a home has 2 or 3 bedrooms, label it `"2 or 3"`
-   If a home has 4 bedrooms, label it `"4"`
-   If a home has 5 or more bedrooms, label it `"5+`

You ask your TA how to implement this logic, and they give you the following data transformation pipeline as a hint.

```{r}
#| eval: false
duke_forest <- duke_forest |>
  __[BLANK 1]__(
    bed_new = __[BLANK 2]__(
      bed == 2 __[BLANK 3]__ bed == 3 ~ "2 or 3",
      bed __[BLANK 4]__ 4             ~ "4",
      bed >= 5                        ~ "5+"
    )
  ) |>
  __[BLANK 5]__(bed, bed_new)
```

The first ten rows and the first few columns of the resulting, updated `duke_forest` data frame are shown below, with the variable types suppressed (since you'll be asked about them later).

```{r}
#| echo: false
duke_forest <- duke_forest |>
  mutate(
    bed_new = case_when(
      bed == 2 | bed == 3 ~ "2 or 3",
      bed == 4            ~ "4",
      bed >= 5            ~ "5+"
    ),
  ) |>
  relocate(bed, bed_new)

format(as_tibble(duke_forest))[-3L] |>
  str_remove_all(" <.*?>") |>
  cat(sep = "\n")
```

A team of five data scientists is working together to explore, model, and make inferences about holiday movies using a dataset on `{r} nrow(holiday_movies)` holiday movies; movies with "holiday", "Christmas", "Hanukkah", or "Kwanzaa" (or variants thereof) in their title.
Each member of the team is responsible for a different part of the analysis.
The data come from the Internet Movie Database (IMDb).
The data frame is called `holiday_movies` and it contains the variables described in the table below.

| Variable | Description |
|:-----------------|:-----------------------------------------------------|
| `id` | IMDb ID of movie |
| `title_type` | Type of the title (Feature Film or TV Movie) |
| `title` | Title used on promotional materials at the point of release |
| `year` | Release year of a title |
| `runtime` | Primary runtime of the title, in minutes |
| `genre` | Primary genre associated with the title |
| `score` | Weighted average of all the individual user ratings on IMDb |
| `num_votes` | Number of votes the title has received on IMDb |
| `christmas` | Whether the title includes "christmas", "xmas", "x mas", etc. |
| `hanukkah` | Whether the title includes "hanukkah", "chanukah", etc. |
| `kwanzaa` | Whether the title includes "kwanzaa" |
| `holiday` | Whether the title includes the word "holiday" |

: {tbl-colwidths="\[20,80\]"}

The density curves below show the distributions of `score`s in Feature Films and TV Movies.
The means are overlaid on these distributions: a mean score of `{r} holiday_ff_mean` for Feature Films and a mean score of `{r} holiday_tv_mean` for TV Movies.

  ) +

    color = "black", fill = "white", size = 4
  ) +
  annotate(
    geom = "segment",

A bootstrap distribution of the difference between the mean scores of holiday TV Movies and Feature Films is generated using the code below:

```{r}
set.seed(1234)

boot_dist <- holiday_movies |>
  specify(score ~ title_type) |>
  generate(reps = 1000, type = "bootstrap") |>
  calculate(
    stat = "diff in means", 
    order = c("TV Movie", "Feature Film")
  )
```


```{r}
#| include: false
ci <- boot_dist |>
  summarize(
    lower = quantile(stat, 0.025),
    upper = quantile(stat, 0.975),
  )
```

The plot below visualizes the bootstrap distribution.
The 95% confidence interval is (0.442, 0.670).
The bounds for this interval are overlaid on the plot.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-asp: 0.5
ggplot(boot_dist, aes(x = stat)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.05, color = "gray") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = round(seq(-0.6, 0.6, 0.1), 1)) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 300, 50)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(ci$lower, ci$upper), linewidth = 1.5)
```

The fourth team member is also working on modeling, but they classifying movies as either Feature Films or TV Movies (`title_type`) based on their `runtime`, `score`, and  `num_votes`.
Their code and output is shown below.

```{r}
# make title_type a factor
holiday_movies <- holiday_movies |>
  mutate(title_type = fct_relevel(title_type, "TV Movie", "Feature Film"))

# split the data into training and testing
set.seed(221)
holiday_movies_split <- initial_split(holiday_movies)
holiday_movies_train <- training(holiday_movies_split)
holiday_movies_test <- testing(holiday_movies_split)

# fit model to training data
title_type_fit <- logistic_reg() |>
  fit(title_type ~ runtime + score + num_votes, data = holiday_movies_train)

# make predictions for testing data
holiday_movies_aug <- augment(title_type_fit, new_data = holiday_movies_test)

# summarize predictions
holiday_movies_aug |>
  count(title_type, .pred_class)
```
